planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown stock in early spring or fall, staking loosely for the first year until roots anchor the vase-shaped canopy.

directions: Zelkova serrata thrives in deep, well-drained loam but tolerates compacted urban soils, heat, and drought far better than American elm once established, making it a favored street-tree substitute since Dutch elm disease decimated elm plantings. Give it an open site with full sun so the graceful vase-shaped crown of arching branches can develop unimpeded; young trees benefit from structural pruning to establish a strong central leader and well-spaced scaffold limbs. Fall color ranges from bronze to red-orange, and the smooth gray bark exfoliates attractively with age. It is largely resistant to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle, and needs only routine watering during establishment and occasional deep soaking in prolonged drought thereafter.
sources: USDA Forest Service Urban Tree Database

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in an open location with room for a wide-spreading vase-shaped canopy; stake young trees loosely for one growing season.

directions: Green Vase was selected for its especially uniform, upright-arching vase silhouette reminiscent of the American elms it was bred to replace, along with faster growth than the species and reliably strong branch angles that resist storm damage. It performs best in full sun on well-drained soil but adapts to clay, compaction, and urban heat, and shows good resistance to Dutch elm disease, elm leaf beetle, and Japanese beetle. Fall foliage turns a dependable rusty red to reddish-purple. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing crossing branches while young, since the cultivar naturally maintains its clean structure with age.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in a spacious full-sun site in spring or fall; this vigorous cultivar quickly outgrows tight parkway strips or small residential lots.

directions: Village Green is one of the older, more vigorous zelkova selections, forming a broad, upright oval crown with a straighter central leader than the species type, and it grows noticeably faster than most other named cultivars. It tolerates heat, drought, alkaline soil, and urban stress once established, and shows strong resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle. Reddish-bronze fall color is consistent and long-lasting. Provide deep, infrequent watering during the first two to three years and prune only to maintain a single dominant leader while the tree is young.
sources: USDA Forest Service Urban Tree Database

planting.note: Plant in full sun along narrow streets or tight urban corridors where its columnar form fits spaces a standard zelkova could not.

directions: Musashino is a distinctly narrow, columnar zelkova selection originating in Japan, with multiple upright trunks that stay tightly fastigiate even at maturity, making it a popular choice for boulevard plantings and confined urban sites where a wide-spreading shade tree would not fit. It tolerates the same range of soils and urban stresses as the species and shares its resistance to Dutch elm disease. Fall color is a warm orange-bronze. Because the form is naturally tight, little corrective pruning is required beyond removing any wayward lateral that disrupts the columnar silhouette.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in a large open site in spring or fall; this massive shade tree is a classic choice for city streets, parks, and boulevards with room to spare.

directions: London Plane, a naturally occurring hybrid between American sycamore and Oriental plane, is prized as one of the toughest large shade trees for polluted, compacted city environments, tolerating road salt, root restriction, and heavy pruning far better than most shade trees. It grows best in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun but adapts to a wide range of conditions once established, developing the same attractive mottled, exfoliating bark as American sycamore. It shows better resistance to anthracnose than the straight sycamore species, though it can still be affected in cool, wet springs. Prune to maintain a strong central leader when young, and expect this tree to eventually need a large canopy allowance, as it is not suited to small residential lots.
sources: USDA Forest Service Urban Tree Database

planting.note: Plant in full sun with ample overhead and root space in spring or fall; this cultivar is bred for improved disease resistance in demanding street-tree settings.

directions: Bloodgood is the most widely planted London Plane selection in North America, chosen for improved resistance to anthracnose and powdery mildew compared with seedling-grown trees, along with vigorous, uniform growth well suited to nursery production and street-tree programs. It shares the species' tolerance of compacted soil, pollution, heat, and road salt, and develops the same showy camouflage-patterned exfoliating bark that makes mature specimens so distinctive in winter. Give it a large uncontested root zone and full sun; established trees need little supplemental water beyond periods of extended drought. Prune in the dormant season to remove crossing limbs and maintain clearance over streets and sidewalks.
sources: USDA Forest Service Urban Tree Database

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall in full sun; this fast-growing, tough elm establishes quickly and adapts to a wide range of soils.

directions: The straight species of Chinese or lacebark elm is valued for its handsome mottled, exfoliating bark in patches of gray, green, orange, and brown, its late-summer bloom of inconspicuous flowers, and its strong natural resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle that plague American and European elms. It grows quickly into a rounded to vase-shaped canopy and tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and urban conditions once established, making it a reliable low-maintenance shade tree across a broad range of climates. In the Gulf South and other mild-winter regions it often holds its small leathery leaves semi-evergreen into winter. Prune while young to remove weak, narrow-angled branch unions, and avoid confusion with the invasive, weak-wooded Siberian elm (Ulmus pumila), which is sometimes mislabeled as Chinese elm in the nursery trade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
USDA Forest Service Urban Tree Database
